title: 21 arrested in alleged Toronto-area towing industry crime ring investigation: police
summary: A joint-police probe targeting an alleged organized crime ring with connections to Toronto’s towing industry has resulted in a total of 112 charges placed on 21 people, including its alleged leader,…

blocks.text: A joint-police probe targeting an alleged organized crime ring with connections to Toronto’s towing industry has resulted in a total of 112 charges placed on 21 people, including its alleged leader, police say.
A conspiracy to commit murder is among the total of 112 charges placed on the accused, police say
Police say 21 people have been arrested as part of an investigation cracking down on alleged organized crime in the Greater Toronto Area towing industry.
A joint-police probe targeting an alleged organized crime ring with connections to Toronto’s towing industry has resulted in 21 arrests, including its alleged leader, police say.

The 21 accused face a collective 112 criminal charges, including several related to firearm trafficking, auto theft, arson and fraudulent physiotherapy clinics, according to police. One employee at a correctional facility has also been charged with breach of trust.

Police allege Manoharan Subramaniam, a 43-year-old from Whitby, was the ringleader of the criminal organization. He and two others each face two charges of conspiracy to commit murder, Insp. Steve Matthews with Toronto Police Service’s guns and gangs task force told reporters at a news conference Wednesday.

Subramaniam is accused of directing a plan to murder two people, also connected to the towing industry. Subramaniam was also allegedly connected to two Greater Toronto Area towing companies police believe were involved in criminal activity, said Matthews.

“We allege that, although ownership and assets were registered to other individuals, Mr. Subramaniam exercised control over aspects of those operations,” Matthews said. He said the companies were Williams Towing and Bob's Towing.

Williams Towing had a contract with Toronto police, Matthews said. The company towed vehicles after police traffic stops, as well as illegally parked vehicles, he said. Police terminated the contract with the company last week, “immediately” after the discovery, said Matthews.
Two dozen search warrants were executed during the probe, dubbed “Project Swords,” including 13 on Nov. 12, police say.
Towing-related crime is going down, say police
Chief Supt. Joe Matthews says the Greater Toronto Area has seen a sharp escalation in crimes linked to the towing industry since early 2023 and police have been working to address it.
He says 62 shooting and firearm incidents were linked to tow-truck disputes in 2024, accounting for nearly 13 per cent of all such incidents in Toronto.
'This is not our industry': Professional Towing Assn. of Ontario | Hanomansing Tonight

The chief superintendent says the number was 18 incidents in 2025, representing seven per cent of all such incidents that year. That's down to five incidents so far this year, accounting for approximately two per cent.
He said "good police work" is one of "multiple factors that can explain fluctuations in gun violence numbers."
"By targeting organized crime groups in these investigations, we have had a direct impact on reducing gun violence in our city."
With files from The Canadian Press
